solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Temporary stable lad unseated here

parts.note: the surface: a racing yard, where a lad has been thrown from his horse at some makeshift stable
the setter's reading: a place in a theatre or stadium where the audience has no seats and must stay on its feet

explanation.surface: A stable lad thrown from his mount at a makeshift yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' and 'unseated' point at horses; read 'unseated' literally as 'without a seat' and 'temporary stable' as a way of being upright for a while.
explanation.definitionFit: Space in a venue sold for spectators who stay upright on their feet because every chair is already taken.

clue.text: In conversation claim female consumed surfeit

indicators.note: words exchanged in conversation are spoken, so we go by how the phrase is said

parts.note: to claim is to say, a female is she, and consumed is ate

explanation.surface: Someone remarking that a woman has eaten far too much.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the three-word phrase quickly and it runs together into the answer; 'surfeit' is the verb here, not the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to surfeit is to feed someone beyond what they need, filling them completely: a direct synonym.

clue.text: Touching answer wins time

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for answer
to win something is to gain it
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A moving reply that buys someone a little more time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touching' looks like 'moving', an adjective about the answer; it is the definition, meaning in contact with, as a ladder leans against a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Something leaning against a wall is in physical contact with it, so the preposition matches the sense of pressed up close.

clue.text: Stay extremely desperate and become alcoholic

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of desperate
juice becomes alcoholic when it ferments

explanation.surface: A plea for someone in despair not to turn to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Become alcoholic' reads as a person's decline; it is sugar turning into alcohol. 'Stay' is the noun, as in a stay of execution.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay is a legal postponement, as of a sentence, and postponing an action is putting it off till later.

clue.text: VIP lifted prohibition of humming

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting something turns its letters upward so they read from the bottom

parts.note: in British slang to hum is to smell bad, and BO is body odour
a ban is a prohibition; a ban of BO is a BO ban

explanation.surface: An important person has cancelled a rule against humming a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humming' suggests a tune; in British slang something that hums smells, hence BO. 'Lifted' looks like cancelled but turns the letters over.
explanation.definitionFit: A nabob was a man who came home rich from India, so the word came to mean any wealthy, important personage.

clue.text: Broken humeri punctured by new metal

indicators.note: a punctured thing has something pushed into its middle, so one piece goes inside another
something broken is in pieces that can be put back in another arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: An X-ray shows broken arm bones pierced by a new metal pin.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a surgical scene, and humeri (upper arm bones) are the fodder; N then drops into the rearranged letters, making the whole answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhenium is a rare, dense chemical element of the transition group, element number 75, so it is a metal.

clue.text: Daring to cycle in front of bad cops

indicators.note: to cycle is to go round, so the first letter rides round to the back
being in front means coming first, so the pieces are placed one before the other

parts.note: daring is bold; send its B round to the end
ill means bad, as in ill will

explanation.surface: A reckless cyclist rides straight in front of some corrupt police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In front of' places the first piece before the second. The Old Bill is British slang for the police.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Bill is a British slang name for the police force collectively, as cops is in American usage.

clue.text: Roaming US states Ohio and Georgia in part

indicators.note: roaming things wander without a fixed order, so the letters move about

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: A road trip through Ohio and Georgia, two American states.
explanation.walkthrough: Georgia looks like the US state beside Ohio; it is the country in the Caucasus, part of whose territory is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: South Ossetia is a breakaway region lying inside Georgia's internationally recognised borders in the Caucasus mountains.

clue.text: Rugby player from Falmouth carelessly knocking out male

indicators.note: doing something carelessly leaves things jumbled out of their proper order
knocking something out removes it, so a letter goes missing

parts.note: the Cornish town, as fodder
M is the abbreviation for male; it is the letter taken away

explanation.surface: A careless rugby player from Falmouth, a Cornish port, flattens an opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove M from the town's letters and shuffle the seven left. 'Knocking out' sounds like a tackle but is the deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: Out-half is another name, used especially in Ireland and Wales, for the fly-half, the back who directs play.

clue.text: Scope of brief article on money

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: bread is slang for money
the article THE, cut short

explanation.surface: Asking how wide-ranging a short piece of writing about finance is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a piece of writing; it is the grammatical article. In an across clue 'on' puts the article after the money.
explanation.definitionFit: Scope is range or extent, and breadth is the width of coverage something has: close synonyms.

clue.text: One embracing criminal secretly

parts.note: one who embraces people hugs them
a mugger is a street robber

explanation.surface: Someone quietly holding a lawbreaker close.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves rhyme, so one leads to the other. As an adverb the answer is old-fashioned for in secret.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugger-mugger, used as an adverb, describes acting covertly and in concealment, an old synonym of in secret.

clue.text: Coach regularly coming from Torbay isn't about to return

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter, taken from the words that follow

parts.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

indicators.note: to return is to come back the way you went, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: re means about, as in business letters

explanation.surface: A coach trip out of Torbay, a Devon resort, that will not be coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' tempts as the bus leaving Torbay; it is a sports coach. The selection runs across two words, apostrophe ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A coach instructs athletes or teams, and a trainer is the person who prepares and drills them: synonyms.

clue.text: Carry cans home for preserving food

indicators.note: a can holds its contents, so one piece keeps another inside it

parts.note: to carry something along is to bring it
at home is in

explanation.surface: Bringing tins back from the shop to stock the larder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cans' looks like tins of food, fitting the surface; it is a verb meaning holds. The home piece sits after BR.
explanation.definitionFit: Brining steeps meat, fish or vegetables in salty water so that they keep for months: a method of preservation.

clue.text: Public penury, essentially

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so its outer letters are stripped off

parts.note: penury is poverty; keep all but its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A remark that being poor in public is the essence of the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: The synonym must be found before the selection: penury becomes a seven-letter word, then loses both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Overt means done openly, not hidden from view, which is what public means when describing an action.

clue.text: Flee Milan, running with loved ones

indicators.note: running things are in motion, so the letters move into a fresh order

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: An escape from Milan, running off together with the family.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is French, borrowed into English; the Italian city makes the phrase look foreign in the wrong language.
explanation.definitionFit: En famille is French for at home among one's relatives, borrowed into English to mean in the family circle.

clue.text: Perhaps William Spooner's cultivated reputation

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts change places

parts.note: to cultivate is to nurse along; its N swaps with the F of the next word
fame is a public reputation; it gives its F to the first word

explanation.surface: Spooner's carefully tended reputation, perhaps belonging to someone called William.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that William is Spooner's own given name, so the definition refers back to the man named in the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: William is an example of a given personal name, the one that comes before a surname like Spooner.

clue.text: Deal for one accepted by great advocate

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: super means great
Deal is a harbour town in Kent, one example of a port

explanation.surface: A lawyer agreeing to a bargain on a client's behalf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deal' is capitalised only because it opens the clue; it is the Kent town, not a bargain. 'For one' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: An advocate speaks up publicly for a cause, and a supporter backs one: synonyms in the sense of champion.

clue.text: Basil perhaps is blind at first after choking smoke

parts.note: pother is an old word for a choking cloud of smoke or dust

indicators.note: at first means at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of blind

explanation.surface: A man called Basil who has gone blind after inhaling thick smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: Basil looks like a name; it is the plant. 'After' puts the letter behind the smoke, and pother is a rare word worth learning.
explanation.definitionFit: A potherb is any plant grown for the cooking pot, and basil is one such culinary herb, so an example.

clue.text: Little-known surgeon supporting oxygen therapy

indicators.note: in a down entry, what supports sits underneath, so it comes later in the answer

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
BS is Bachelor of Surgery, a surgeon's qualification
a therapy aims to be a cure

explanation.surface: An unknown surgeon who backs oxygen treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting oxygen therapy' reads as a single medical treatment; split it, with the surgeon below the gas and the therapy after.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obscure is not widely recognised or famous, which is what little-known means: a straight synonym.

clue.text: Very oddly observed, loves motorway and noise of cars

indicators.note: looking only at the odd positions keeps the first, third and so on

parts.note: the first and third letters
love is zero in tennis, so two loves are two Os
M is for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: Someone oddly fond of motorways and the roar of traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loves' reads as a verb; it is the plural of love, a zero score. British motorways are numbered M1, M25 and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Vroom imitates the roar of an engine revving or a vehicle speeding off, a sound made by motors.

clue.text: Harridans with spirit ousting earlier maidens

indicators.note: to oust is to push out and take the place of, so one piece swaps in for another

parts.note: a virago is a domineering woman
gin is a spirit
ago means earlier, in the past; these letters leave

explanation.surface: Fierce old women drinking spirits, driving out the young girls who came before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' can suggest temperament; it is the drink. 'Earlier' looks like it modifies maidens, but it is the piece being removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Maiden is an old word for a young unmarried woman, traditionally presumed to be a virgin, hence the synonym.

clue.text: View tear-jerker about end of Philip I

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: chopping an onion brings tears to the eyes

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, which is the one kept

parts.note: its final letter
taken as it stands

explanation.surface: Watching a weepy film about the death of King Philip I.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear-jerker' suggests a sad film; it is the vegetable. 'Philip I' reads as a king's name, but the I is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A view is a personal belief or judgement on a matter, as in 'in my view', which is an opinion.

clue.text: Child with poor seat for As You Like It

indicators.note: something in poor shape is out of order and needs rearranging

parts.note: a tot is a small child
anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: A child stuck in a bad seat at a performance of Shakespeare's comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make it look like the play's title, but it is the everyday phrase, as a recipe says salt as you like it.
explanation.definitionFit: A recipe saying season to taste lets the cook add as much as they prefer, which is the phrase's everyday meaning.

clue.text: Acclaim some rising digital celebrities

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising goes upward, so the letters read from the bottom
some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters lie within the words

parts.note: the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Praise for a few up-and-coming online influencers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' fits celebrities on the way up; in a down clue it turns the letters upward. The answer is borrowed from French.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat means brilliant success or great public applause, so it overlaps with praise and renown.

clue.text: Go to bed with gigolos, initially in rotation

parts.note: to turn in is to go to bed

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Sleeping with one hired lover after another, taking them in turns.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is racy, but 'go to bed' is simply retiring for the night, and 'with' just adds the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something turning is spinning round an axis, which is what being in rotation means: a direct paraphrase.

clue.text: Topless worker occasionally cuddling former partner without desire

indicators.note: without a top means the first letter is gone
to cuddle is to hold close in your arms, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: a casual is an occasional worker; drop its first letter
an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: A topless worker hugging an ex, yet feeling nothing for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' looks like an alternate-letter instruction; it belongs with 'worker' to give the occasional worker.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone asexual feels no sexual attraction to others, so they are free of that longing or lust.

clue.text: Idiotic Head of Accounts is retiring before watershed?

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the letters run the other way
the head of a word is its top, so its opening letter is kept

parts.note: its opening letter
the word itself, turned round
the British TV watershed is 9pm, before which adult content is kept off air

explanation.surface: A foolish head of finance goes to bed before the evening news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of Accounts' looks like a job title. The watershed is the 9pm cut-off on British television, after which adult content may be shown.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means donkey-like, from Latin asinus, and so stupid or foolish in the extreme.

clue.text: Lacking purpose, once missing church for example

parts.note: an object is a purpose, and without one is objectless

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so a letter drops out

parts.note: the word itself, before letters go
CE is the Church of England; these letters are taken away

explanation.surface: Someone who once had a purpose but stopped going to church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking purpose' reads as the definition; it is the first piece, and the definition is the last word, 'example'.
explanation.definitionFit: An object lesson is a vivid practical illustration of a principle, a model instance to learn from.
